q: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust.
e: Oxygen is indeed the most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

q: The free element of oxygen accounts for 21% of the mass of the atmosphere.
e: The free element of oxygen accounts for 21% of the volume, not the mass, of the atmosphere.

q: Oxygen in the combined state exists in water, sand or silica, silicates and rocks.
e: This is the exact description of oxygen's combined state in nature.

q: Potassium chlorate should be used for the preparation of oxygen in the laboratory because it is environmentally friendly.
e: Potassium chlorate is principally toxic by injection and inhalation, so it should not be used.

q: In the preparation of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide, manganese(IV) oxide is used as a catalyst to speed up the chemical reaction.
e: Manganese(IV) oxide acts as a catalyst in this environmentally friendly preparation method.

q: Oxygen gas is collected by the upward displacement of water.
e: Oxygen gas is collected by the downward displacement of water.

q: Oxygen is a colourless gas, without taste or smell.
e: These are the standard physical properties of oxygen gas.

q: Oxygen is highly soluble in water.
e: Oxygen is only slightly soluble in water.

q: Oxygen will not burn, however, it supports combustion.
e: Oxygen itself does not burn but is essential for supporting combustion.

q: Oxygen rekindles any glowing thing with a bright flame.
e: This is a standard test for the presence of oxygen gas.

q: Metals such as magnesium, iron, copper and zinc react with oxygen forming oxides.
e: These metals react with oxygen to form their respective metal oxides.

q: A piece of clean magnesium ribbon continues burning in oxygen from air with a dazzling white flame, leaving a black powder as residue.
e: It leaves a white powder (magnesium oxide) as residue, not a black powder.

q: Iron slowly becomes oxidised in the presence of air and water, to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, i.e., iron has become rusted.
e: This is the chemical process of rusting.

q: Non-metals such as phosphorus, sulphur and carbon react with oxygen forming oxides.
e: These non-metals undergo combustion in oxygen to form their respective oxides.

q: A small piece of white phosphorus burns in oxygen giving off white fumes which consist of oxides of phosphorus.
e: Only red phosphorus may be used for this demonstration, not white phosphorus.

q: An oxide is a compound containing oxygen and another element.
e: This is the fundamental definition of an oxide.

q: There are six types of oxides.
e: The six types are acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, peroxides, and compound oxides.

q: An acidic oxide is an oxide of metal.
e: An acidic oxide is an oxide of a non-metal.

q: Acidic oxides react with alkali solutions to give salts and water.
e: This neutralization reaction is a defining property of acidic oxides.

q: $CO_2$, $SO_2$, $SO_3$ and $P_4O_{10}$ are insoluble acidic oxides.
e: $CO_2$, $SO_2$, $SO_3$ and $P_4O_{10}$ are soluble acidic oxides.

q: $SiO_2$ is an insoluble acidic oxide.
e: Silicon dioxide is a notable exception as an insoluble acidic oxide.

q: Soluble acidic oxides dissolve in water to form acidic solutions that turn blue litmus red.
e: This is the standard indicator test for acidic solutions.

q: A basic oxide is an oxide of non-metal.
e: A basic oxide is an oxide of a metal.

q: A basic oxide reacts with an acid to produce a salt and water only.
e: This neutralization reaction is a defining property of basic oxides.

q: $Na_2O$ and $K_2O$ are insoluble basic oxides.
e: $Na_2O$ and $K_2O$ are soluble basic oxides.

q: $MgO$, $CuO$ and $Ag_2O$ are insoluble basic oxides.
e: These metal oxides do not dissolve readily in water.

q: Some basic oxides react with water forming hydroxide solutions that turn red litmus blue.
e: These hydroxide solutions are alkalis, which turn red litmus blue.

q: An amphoteric oxide is a metallic oxide which possesses both basic and acidic properties.
e: This is the exact definition of an amphoteric oxide.

q: An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis to form salt and water.
e: This dual reactivity is the hallmark of amphoteric oxides.

q: $ZnO$, $Al_2O_3$ and $PbO$ are examples of amphoteric oxides.
e: These are the standard examples of amphoteric oxides provided in the text.

q: The neutral oxide is an oxide which shows neither basic nor acidic character.
e: This is the definition of a neutral oxide.

q: $CO$ and $N_2O$ are examples of neutral oxides.
e: Carbon monoxide and nitrous oxide are classic examples of neutral oxides.

q: Peroxides are oxides that react with an acid to give salt and water only.
e: Peroxides react with an acid to give salt and hydrogen peroxide.

q: $BaO_2$ and $Na_2O_2$ are examples of peroxides.
e: Barium peroxide and sodium peroxide are standard examples of peroxides.

q: $PbO_2$, $MnO_2$ and $NO_2$ are peroxides.
e: $PbO_2$, $MnO_2$ and $NO_2$ are not peroxides; they do not give hydrogen peroxides on reaction with acids.

q: A compound oxide is an oxide, formed by the combination of two different oxides of the same element.
e: This is the exact definition of a compound oxide.

q: $Pb_3O_4$, $Mn_3O_4$ and $Fe_3O_4$ are examples of compound oxides.
e: These are the standard examples of compound oxides.

q: $Pb_3O_4$ is a compound oxide consisting of lead(II) and lead(IV) oxides.
e: It can be written as di-lead(II) lead(IV) oxide or red lead oxide ($2PbO \cdot PbO_2$).

q: When red lead oxide reacts with dilute nitric acid, lead(IV) oxide only reacts with the acid to form lead(II) nitrate.
e: Only the lead(II) oxide portion reacts with the acid to form lead(II) nitrate.

q: Man and animals use oxygen from the air in respiration.
e: Oxygen is essential for the respiration process in living organisms.

q: Liquid oxygen is carried on rockets to support the fuel burns.
e: Liquid oxygen serves as an oxidizer in rocket propulsion.

q: $CO_2$ is used as a bleaching agent.
e: $CO_2$ is used in fire extinguishers; $SO_2$ is used as a bleaching agent.

q: $MgO$ is used as a laxative.
e: Magnesium oxide has medicinal uses including as a laxative.

q: $CaO$ is used in cement production.
e: Calcium oxide is a key raw material in the manufacture of cement.

q: $SiO_2$ is used in the manufacture of glass.
e: Silicon dioxide is the primary component in glass manufacturing.

q: $Pb_3O_4$ is used as a pigment used in paints.
e: Red lead oxide is commonly used as a pigment in paints.

q: $ZnO$ is used as skin conditioners and cosmetics.
e: Zinc oxide is widely used in dermatological and cosmetic products.

q: $H_2O_2$ is used as an antiseptic, in hair dyes and toothpaste.
e: Hydrogen peroxide has these specific commercial and medical applications.

q: Carbon is found in nature as diamond and graphite.
e: Diamond and graphite are the natural crystalline forms of carbon.

q: Fullerene and graphene are natural forms of carbon.
e: Fullerene and graphene are synthetic forms of carbon.

q: Carbon can be found as compounds combining with other elements in petroleum, coal, natural gas, limestone, carbon dioxide and sugar ($C_2H_2O_{11}$).
e: This lists the common natural and compound occurrences of carbon as stated in the text.

q: If an element can exist in more than one form, in the same physical state, it is said to exhibit allotropy or polymorphism.
e: This is the exact definition of allotropy or polymorphism.

q: The different forms of an element in the same physical state that possess different chemical properties are known as allotropes of that element.
e: Allotropes possess different physical properties, though they may have different chemical properties.

q: Diamond, graphite, fullerene and graphene are allotropes of carbon.
e: These are the four main allotropes of carbon discussed.

q: Oxygen and ozone are allotropes of oxygen.
e: Oxygen ($O_2$) and ozone ($O_3$) are allotropes of the element oxygen.

q: Rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur are allotropes of sulphur.
e: These are the two common allotropes of sulphur.

q: In diamond, each carbon atom is surrounded by three other carbon atoms.
e: In diamond, each carbon atom is surrounded by four other carbon atoms.

q: Diamond has a giant structure containing millions of carbon atoms in a three dimensional network of strong carbon-carbon covalent bonds.
e: This 3D covalent network is responsible for diamond's extreme hardness.

q: Diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point of 3550 °C.
e: The strong covalent bonds give diamond this exceptionally high melting point.

q: Diamond is the hardest among all naturally occurring substances.
e: This is a well-known physical property of diamond.

q: In graphite, each carbon atom is surrounded by three other carbon atoms in the same plane, and therefore layers of hexagons are obtained.
e: This planar arrangement creates the layered structure of graphite.

q: In graphite, the distance between the layers is less than the distance between adjacent carbon atoms.
e: The distance between the layers is more than the distance between adjacent carbon atoms.

q: Due to its layered structure, graphite is soft and has soapy touch.
e: The weak bonding between layers allows them to slide over each other.

q: The layers in graphite are bonded through strong covalent forces known as van der Waals forces.
e: The layers are bonded through weak forces known as van der Waals forces.

q: Due to the presence of free electrons, graphite is a good conductor of electricity and heat.
e: The delocalized electrons in graphite allow for electrical and thermal conductivity.

q: The melting point of graphite is 3700 °C.
e: Graphite has an even higher melting point than diamond due to its extensive covalent network within layers.

q: Fullerene ($C_{60}$) is an allotrope of carbon in the form of a hollow sphere, ellipsoid, tube and many other shapes and sizes.
e: Fullerenes can take various geometric forms.

q: Spherical fullerenes are also referred to as Bucky balls.
e: This is the common nickname for spherical fullerenes.

q: Cylindrical fullerenes are also called carbon nanotubes.
e: This is the correct terminology for cylindrical fullerenes.

q: Fullerenes can be found abundantly in nature.
e: Fullerenes cannot be found in nature; they are synthetic allotropes of carbon.

q: Fullerenes have lower melting and boiling points than diamond and graphite.
e: As molecular structures, fullerenes have lower melting and boiling points than the giant covalent structures of diamond and graphite.

q: Graphene is a single layer (monolayer) of graphite.
e: This is the exact definition of graphene.

q: Graphene has a three-dimensional crystalline structure.
e: Graphene has a two-dimensional crystalline structure.

q: In proportion to its thickness, graphene is about 100 times stronger than the strongest steel.
e: This highlights the exceptional tensile strength of graphene.

q: Graphene is a transparent and flexible conductor.
e: These properties make it highly valuable for modern electronic applications.

q: Charcoal, coal, coke and carbon black (soot) are assumed to be amorphous forms of carbon.
e: These are traditionally classified as amorphous carbon.

q: These amorphous forms of carbon contain randomly oriented small crystals of graphite.
e: Modern analysis shows they are not truly amorphous but contain microcrystalline graphite.

q: Charcoal is made by heating wood in the presence of air.
e: Charcoal is made by heating wood in the absence of air.

q: Charcoal has a porous structure and has many small holes.
e: This porous nature gives charcoal its adsorptive properties.

q: Coal is found in nature and is a black heavy solid.
e: Coal is a naturally occurring fossil fuel with these physical characteristics.

q: Coke is formed by heating coal in the presence of air.
e: Coke is formed by heating coal in the absence of air.

q: Coke is almost pure carbon.
e: The destructive distillation of coal removes volatile impurities, leaving nearly pure carbon.

q: Carbon black (soot) is a black powder left when kerosene is burnt in a limited amount of air.
e: Incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons like kerosene produces carbon black.

q: When carbon burns in excess air or oxygen, carbon monoxide is formed.
e: When carbon burns in excess air or oxygen, carbon dioxide is formed.

q: Carbon monoxide is formed when carbon burns in a limited amount of air or oxygen.
e: Incomplete combustion due to limited oxygen produces carbon monoxide.

q: Carbon can be used as a reducing agent in the extraction of some metals.
e: Carbon's ability to remove oxygen from metal oxides makes it a valuable reducing agent.

q: When strongly heated, carbon can reduce the oxides of zinc and other metals such as $CuO$, $PbO$ and $Fe_2O_3$ to their respective metals.
e: This is a standard metallurgical application of carbon.

q: Carbon is a major component of giant molecules called macromolecules which include proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and carbohydrates.
e: This highlights carbon's fundamental role in biological chemistry.

q: Diamond is used for jewellery because of its brilliant shine.
e: Its high refractive index and dispersion give diamond its brilliant shine.

q: Powdered graphite is used as dry lubricant for machine parts which operate at high temperature because graphite is volatile.
e: Graphite is used as a high-temperature lubricant because it is non-volatile.

q: Graphite crucibles are used as containers for melting metals at high temperature.
e: Graphite's high melting point and thermal stability make it ideal for crucibles.

q: Fullerene is used in artificial photosynthesis, cosmetics, surface coating of medical devices and drug delivery system.
e: These are the specific modern applications of fullerene listed in the text.

q: Graphene is widely used for solar cells, light-emitting diodes (LED), touch panels and smart windows or phones.
e: Graphene's transparency and conductivity enable these advanced electronic applications.

q: Activated charcoal is used as adsorbent in industry for bleaching, deodourization of substances and in water purification.
e: The porous structure of activated charcoal gives it excellent adsorptive properties.

q: Coal is used as a fuel and also used to produce coke and coal tar.
e: These are the primary industrial uses of coal.

q: Coke is used as a fuel in metal industry and as reducing agent in the extraction of metals.
e: Coke is essential in blast furnaces for both heat and reduction.

q: Carbon black is used for making printing ink, black shoes polish and as filler in vehicle tyres and other rubber products.
e: These are the standard commercial applications of carbon black.
